title: HTTPS and the Padlock
about: How your connection to a website is kept secret, and what the padlock means.

cards.prompt:
You're on café Wi-Fi, logging in to a site that uses **plain [[HTTP]]** (no S). Your [[packets|packet]] pass through the café's [[router]], then your provider's routers, then a string of others owned by people you've never met.

Who could read your password on its way?

options.text: Anyone who controls a device along the route, like the café's router
Only the website's server, because the password is addressed to it
options.nudge: An address on a packet doesn't stop others reading it, any more than an address on a postcard does. Who handles it on the way?

options.text: Nobody, because the password box hides what you type
options.nudge: The dots only hide your password on your screen. On the network, plain HTTP travels as readable text.

options.text: Only the café, since its Wi-Fi is the one you joined
options.nudge: The café's router is only the first stop. Your packets pass through many more routers after it.

cards.explanation: Plain HTTP is like a **postcard**: the password travels as readable text through **every** device on the route, from the café's router to your provider's routers and beyond. The dots you see when typing only hide it on your screen, not on the [[network]].
cards.hint: Think of plain HTTP as a postcard. Who gets to handle a postcard on its way to the address?

cards.title: HTTPS: HTTP in a locked box
cards.body:
**HTTPS** is the same [[HTTP]], carried inside another [[protocol]] called **TLS**. TLS **encrypts** the data: it scrambles it with secret keys that only your [[browser]] and the [[server]] have. To every router in between, it looks like random noise.

HTTPS uses [[port]] **443** (plain HTTP uses 80), and your browser shows a **padlock** beside the address.

cards.prompt:
Before any [[HTTP]] travels, TLS does a [[handshake]] of its own. The two sides agree secret keys, and the server shows its **certificate**: a digital ID card saying "I really am example.com". A **certificate authority**, an organisation your [[browser]] trusts, issued it after checking who owns that name.

Put the steps of loading an HTTPS page in order.

items.label: TLS handshake: keys agreed and the certificate checked
The browser sends an encrypted GET request
The server sends back an encrypted response

cards.explanation: TCP opens the connection first ("Can we talk?", "Yes, can you hear me?", "Yes"). Then the **TLS handshake** agrees the keys and checks the certificate. Only then does any HTTP travel, and all of it is encrypted.
cards.hint: A connection has to be open before it can be made secure, and it has to be secure before anything private travels.
cards.nudge: TLS can't start until TCP's connection is open. And the request can't be encrypted until the keys are agreed.

cards.prompt: Match each thing you want to the part of [[HTTPS]] that does it.

pairs.left: Stop the café reading your password
Prove the server really is example.com
Vouch that a certificate is genuine
Check at a glance that you're encrypted

cards.explanation: **Encryption** keeps what you send private on the way. The **certificate** is the server's ID card, and a **certificate authority** is who vouches for that ID. The **padlock** is your browser's quick sign that the connection is encrypted.
cards.hint: One is scrambling, one is an ID card, one is whoever issues ID cards, and one is an icon in the address bar.
cards.nudge: Don't mix up the ID card with who issues it: the server shows its certificate, and the certificate authority vouches for it.

cards.prompt:
A padlock means just two things: the connection is encrypted, and the server proved with its certificate that it owns the **name in the address**. It says nothing about who's behind that name, or whether they're honest.

This page shows a padlock. Tap the **one** thing on it that the padlock really vouches for.
cards.explanation: The certificate only backs up the **address**: this server really does belong to whoever owns `login-check.example`. The logo, the warning banner and the boxes are just things drawn on the page, and anyone can draw a bank's name. Here the padlock is real, but the site isn't Your Bank at all.
cards.hint: A certificate is an ID card for a name. Which part of the page shows the site's name, as opposed to what the page says about itself?
cards.nudge: The logo and the banner are just parts of the page that anyone could draw. The certificate is about something your browser shows, not the page.

cards.prompt: You land on a login page at `examp1e.com` (with a digit 1), and it shows a **padlock**. What does the padlock prove?

options.text: Encrypted, to a server that owns examp1e.com: not who runs it
That it's really example.com, checked by a certificate authority
options.nudge: Look again at the name: it has a digit 1. Whoever owns that lookalike name can get a certificate for it.

options.text: That it's safe to type your password, since nobody can read it
options.nudge: Nobody in between can read it, true. But whoever runs this site still gets it at the other end.

options.text: That your browser has checked the site and found no scams on it
options.nudge: The padlock isn't a scam check. It tells you about the connection and the name, not about who runs the site.

cards.explanation: The padlock proves your connection is encrypted, to a server that really owns the exact name **examp1e.com**: whoever registered that lookalike name. It says nothing about whether they're honest, and it's certainly not the real example.com. Nobody can read what you type on the way, but the scammer receives it at the other end.
cards.hint: Read the name closely: is it really example.com? Then remember the two things a padlock means.

cards.prompt:
With HTTPS, the whole HTTP request is encrypted, including the path. But every [[packet]] still carries the server's [[IP address]] on the outside, or routers couldn't deliver it. The site's **name** usually shows too: in your [[DNS]] lookup and at the start of the secure connection.

On café Wi-Fi you open `https://example.com/account/settings` and change your password. What can the café's [[network]] most likely see?

options.text: Which site you're on, but not the page or what you type

options.nudge: The address starts with `https`, so what you send is encrypted. The café can't read your new password.

options.text: The page /account/settings, but not the new password
options.nudge: The path is part of the HTTP request, and with HTTPS the whole request is encrypted.

options.text: Nothing at all, not even which site you're on
options.nudge: Packets still need an address on the outside to be delivered. What does that address give away?

cards.explanation: The **path** and everything you type are inside the [[encrypted|encryption]] request, so they're hidden. But the server's address is on every packet, and the name usually shows up too, in your DNS lookup and at the start of the TLS [[handshake]]. So the café can usually tell **which site**, but not which page or what you send.
cards.hint: Split it into what's inside the encrypted request and what has to stay on the outside of each packet.

cards.prompt: A certificate only counts if it's within its valid dates, written for the name you visited, and issued by a certificate authority your [[browser]] trusts. If a check fails, the browser warns you. Match each warning to what went wrong.

pairs.right: Its valid dates have run out
It was issued for a different name
No trusted authority vouches for it

cards.explanation: Each warning means one check failed: the **dates**, the **name**, or a **trusted issuer**. On a site where you'd log in or pay, don't click past the warning.
cards.hint: Three checks, three warnings: dates, names, and who issued it.
cards.nudge: Read each warning's own words: one is about time, one is about the name, and one is about who issued it.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **HTTPS** is [[HTTP]] inside **TLS**: encrypted between [[browser]] and [[server]].
- A **certificate** proves the server owns the name in the address.
- The padlock means **encrypted**, not **honest**: scam sites have one too.

Next: the grand tour. Everything in this course, in one click.
